title: Lacing leather through punched holes with a running stitch
subtitle: Punch a row of holes and lace a flat leather thong through them in a running stitch to join two pieces of leather or decorate an edge
excerpt: How to lace leather with a flat thong using a running stitch. Covers punching the holes at consistent spacing, choosing the right thong width, and running the lace in and out cleanly.
sourceNotes: UK leatherwork trade practice. City and Guilds leatherwork syllabi (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin, flat strip of leather used for lacing through punched holes. Available in 2 mm, 3 mm, and 4 mm widths in veg-tan, suede, and dyed leather. Thicker and wider than a round cord; the flat face of the thong shows on the face side of the work when laced.

A simple stitch in which the lace passes through consecutive holes alternately from the front to the back and from the back to the front. Produces a dashed line on both faces. The simplest lacing pattern; used for joining two pieces edge-to-edge or for decorative borders.

needs only a row of evenly spaced holes and a length of thong. The technique is used for joining two leather panels edge-to-edge, finishing a belt or strap edge, or for decoration.
Punch the holes at consistent spacing

Mark the hole line with a wing divider set 5 to 6 mm from the edge. Mark hole positions at 6 to 8 mm spacing with a pencil. Use a round punch sized to the thong width: for a 3 mm thong, a 3 mm or 3.5 mm punch allows the thong to pass without puckering. Punch every hole cleanly on a piece of scrap wood. When joining two pieces, punch both at the same time by aligning them edge-to-edge and punching through both layers.

Cut the thong to approximately three times the length of the stitch run, plus a little extra. Skive (thin) the last 10 mm at the starting end to a taper so it passes through the first hole easily. A flat lacing needle (a wide, blunt needle designed for flat thong) threads the thong and makes lacing faster and cleaner, particularly in tight holes.

Start at one end, passing the thong through the first hole from the back to the front, leaving a 20 mm tail on the back. Then pass through the second hole from front to back, the third hole from back to front, and so on. Keep the thong flat and untwisted at every step; a twist shows on the face. Pull each stitch snug but do not distort the leather. At the end, pass the tail through the last hole and back under the last few stitches on the back face.
What it looks like when it is right

On the face: a regular dashed line of flat thong at consistent spacing, with the grain (smooth) side of the thong showing at each pass. The face of the thong should look the same at every hole. On the back: the same pattern in reverse. Irregular spacing or twisting of the thong at any hole is the most common mistake; work slowly and check each stitch before pulling tight.
Punching holes too close to the edge: the leather splits between the hole and the edge when the thong is pulled tight. Minimum distance from edge to hole centre: 5 mm.
Using a thong too wide for the hole: the leather around the hole bulges and the stitches are uneven. Size the punch to the thong.
Not securing the tail at the start: the first stitch works loose. Lock the starting tail under the first two face stitches by running the thong back through them on the back face before continuing.
